parsed_answer.content: Inversion of Control (IoC) is a design principle that shifts the responsibility of object creation and lifecycle management from the application code to a framework or container. In traditional programming, your classes instantiate their dependencies using the 'new' keyword, creating tight coupling that makes unit testing and modularity nearly impossible. IoC inverts this flow: instead of your class asking for a dependency, the framework 'injects' it at runtime. Dependency Injection (DI) is the specific design pattern used to implement IoC. It is the mechanism by which the IoC container provides the necessary objects (beans) to a class. By decoupling the 'what' (the dependency) from the 'how' (the instantiation logic), DI enables loose coupling, allowing developers to swap implementations—such as switching from a MySQL repository to a Mock repository—without modifying the business logic.

items: The Spring IoC Container acts as the orchestrator, reading configuration metadata (via @Component, @Configuration, or XML) to instantiate, configure, and assemble beans.

Constructor Injection is the preferred DI method in production because it ensures the object is always in a valid, fully initialized state and facilitates immutability by allowing the use of 'final' fields.

Field Injection (using @Autowired on private fields) is generally discouraged as it hides dependencies, makes testing harder by requiring reflection, and can lead to NullPointerExceptions if the bean is not correctly initialized.
The Container manages the bean lifecycle, including post-initialization callbacks (@PostConstruct) and destruction hooks, ensuring resources like database connections are cleaned up gracefully.

parsed_answer.content: A common production trap is Circular Dependency. If Bean A requires Bean B, and Bean B requires Bean A, the Spring context will fail to start. While setter injection or @Lazy can technically resolve this, it is almost always a code smell indicating that your classes have too many responsibilities. If you find yourself needing @Lazy, refactor your architecture to extract the shared dependency into a third, independent service.
